reading.body:
Element Critical CH1 publishes 7 MW of IT capacity across 151,000 square feet in Wood Dale, Illinois, ranking fifth among the six Illinois facilities that disclose power figures and contributing less than 3 percent of the state's published 236 MW total.

The facility's large footprint relative to its power output suggests it was built for lower-density, mixed workloads rather than modern GPU clusters, which demand 40 kW per rack or higher. At that density, 7 MW supports roughly 175 racks, but the square footage implies the campus was not originally optimized for such concentration. This distinction matters because AI training is remaking data center economics, and facilities built for traditional enterprise computing often lack the electrical infrastructure, cooling design, and spatial efficiency that high-density GPU deployments require.

PCI DSS and HIPAA certifications confirm the campus targets regulated workloads in payments and healthcare. Neither certification tracks AI capability. The certifications tell you the operator prioritizes compliance-driven tenants, not that the facility does or does not support AI training or inference.

The data does not disclose whether CH1 currently hosts AI workloads, its utilization rate, or future expansion plans. It does not explain why Illinois, despite its location relative to major tech hubs and power infrastructure, publishes so little disclosed capacity compared to other states. Whether this reflects actual scarcity of AI-capable facilities or merely incomplete public disclosure remains unknown.
